slides.title: Three Admin Surfaces — Why RBAC Requires Human Decision
slides.subtitle: Project Setup · Employee Setup · User Management

list.name: Project Setup
list.desc: Create, edit, archive projects. Defines the project taxonomy. AI cannot determine whether the client organisation groups by client name, by domain, or by cost centre. The Lead decides, then prompts.

list.name: Employee Setup
list.desc: Employee directory — the canonical 'personnel of record'. Includes employee number, name, email, active flag. Drives every issue's assignee and reporter selectors.

list.name: User Management
list.desc: Login accounts mapped to Employees. Role assignment. Activation and deactivation. Password reset. AI has no knowledge of the organisational chart; the Lead maps it.

list.name: RBAC matrix
list.desc: The cross-product. Which role exercises which capability across these surfaces. Reporters cannot delete projects. Managers can. Admin retains full authority including user deletion (per FDD §17).

slides.memory_hook: Three surfaces plus RBAC equal the organisational chart in code. AI implements the surfaces. The Lead defines the RBAC.
slides.closing_thread: The admin prompt approach follows.

slides.title: The Admin Prompt — One Prompt Per Surface
slides.subtitle: Same eight-component intent · RBAC clause is invariant
bullets: Unlike the workflow engine (a single extended prompt), admin surfaces are best produced via three focused prompts — one per surface.
Rationale — each surface presents distinct RBAC, validation, and list/detail UX. Decomposition maintains prompt tightness.
Every admin prompt must include — 'RBAC: which role performs which action (matrix below). Server enforces at every endpoint. UI conceals actions a role cannot perform.'
Sample RBAC clause for Project Setup — 'Admin: full CRUD. Manager: full CRUD on accessible projects. Reporter: read-only on accessible projects. Server-side check at the controller layer.'
Commit after each surface validates. Three surfaces — three commits — three push events on Day 6.
slides.memory_hook: Three surfaces · three prompts · three RBAC clauses · three commits. Tight, focused, auditable.
slides.closing_thread: Day 6 afternoon addresses Reports.

slides.title: Day 6 Afternoon — Reports
slides.subtitle: The first artefact the client's executive will examine
slides.opening_hook: Dashboards serve operational users. Reports serve executives. The executive opens a single Excel attachment — the report must perform.
bullets: Eight reports specified in the Issue Tracker FDD — executive summary, by project, by reporter, by assignee, overdue aging, full register, weekly trend, priority matrix.
Every report produces TWO outputs — Excel and PDF. Both must render. Both must meet executive standards.
Filters available on every report — project, date range, status, type. Server applies filters; results do not leak across tenants.
Reports are the artefact the client's executive examines. They convey the narrative the dashboard cannot present on a single screen.

slides.title: The Reports Prompt — Excel and PDF in One Pass
slides.subtitle: References FDD §18 · uses exceljs + pdfkit · cached by query hash

hero_stat.label: × 2 formats (Excel and PDF) × 4 filters each = 64 report variations · produced from one reports module prompt

slides.title: Common Report Defects — Pre-QA Detection
slides.subtitle: Five recurring AI report defects · each preventable via manual inspection

table.orch: ✅ Date columns formatted as dates, numbers as numbers, currency with currency formatting
✅ Header repeated on each page; no orphan rows
✅ Prisma where-clause scopes by user.tenantId on every report query
✅ Reporter names, assignee names, project names — UUIDs never appear in executive reports
✅ Prisma raw SQL + indexes + LIMIT cap (e.g. 50k) with annotation in subtitle

slides.memory_hook: Manually open every report in Excel and PDF before declaring complete. AI handles structure competently; finish requires human verification.
slides.closing_thread: Reports shipped. The handoff to QA follows.
slides.narration: Five common AI report defects. Excel column types stored as text. PDF page breaks splitting rows. Tenant leakage exposing all projects. Internal IDs exposed in client-facing columns. Performance — thirty seconds for ten thousand rows. Open every report manually in Excel and PDF before declaring complete.

narration_script.speaker: Anjali
narration_script.text: Five recurring AI report defects. Each is preventable via manual inspection prior to QA discovery.

narration_script.speaker: Vikram
narration_script.text: First — Excel column types. AI defaults to storing all values as text. Re-prompt — date columns formatted as dates, numbers as numbers, currency with currency formatting.

narration_script.speaker: Anjali
narration_script.text: Second — PDF page breaks. Rows split across pages mid-cell. Header repeated on each page. No orphan rows. Third — tenant leakage. Manager observes all projects globally. Re-prompt the where-clause scoping.

narration_script.speaker: Vikram
narration_script.text: Fourth — internal IDs exposed. UUIDs visible in client-facing columns. Unacceptable. Use reporter names, assignee names, project names.

narration_script.speaker: Anjali
narration_script.text: Fifth — performance. Thirty seconds for ten thousand rows. Prisma raw SQL plus indexes plus a LIMIT cap with annotation in the subtitle. AI handles structure competently; finish requires human verification.

slides.title: Day 7 — The Handoff to QA
slides.subtitle: The collaboration model — not a transfer, a partnership
slides.opening_hook: Conventional engineering transfers builds to QA as if discharging responsibility. OrchestrAI Leads sit with QA throughout testing.

Conventional model — engineer transfers build, QA logs 47 defects, one week of remediation pain.
OrchestrAI model — engineer SITS with QA. Observes testing. Re-prompts in real time as defects surface. Defects close in minutes, not days.

slides.title: The Smoke Checklist — Daily 15-Minute Discipline
slides.subtitle: Nine cases. Every build. Pre-deployment. Invariant.

hero_stat.label: the daily smoke checklist · 9 cases · detects 80% of regressions prior to deployment

bullets: AUTH-001 — Login (valid email plus password → dashboard, JWT stored)
DASH-001 — Dashboard loads, four cards populated, no console errors
ISSA-001 + ISSA-007 — Issue list loads + detail opens with correct identifier
ISNEW-001 — Create issue (happy path), defect number assigned, appears in list
CMT-002 — Post comment with current status (no transition record)
CMT-003 — Post comment with new status (transition triggered, audit log recorded)
PWD-001 — Change password functions, login with new password succeeds
RBAC — Reporter visits /reports → redirected (route guard functions)
RPT-006 — Full issue register opens, exports to Excel and PDF cleanly

slides.title: UAT With the Client — Collaboration, Not Gatekeeping
slides.subtitle: The client is not validating completed work; the client is shaping the product
bullets: UAT occurs with the CLIENT in attendance (in person or screen-share). The Lead operates the application; the client observes and reacts.
Authentic client feedback in OrchestrAI engagements is rarely 'this is broken'. It is more commonly 'this is correct but I prefer it differently'.
Practitioner note — when the client requests capability X that is in scope, respond in the moment with a re-prompt. Demonstrate within five minutes.
When capability X is out of scope — log it; propose phase 2. Avoid both refusal and over-commitment. 'This is a valuable addition; here is how we sequence it.'
UAT sign-off equates to internal client championship. The client communicates to executive leadership — 'this team delivered in seven days what we had awaited for seven months'.

hero_stat.label: comprehensive READMEs · title plus badges · quickstart · features · tech stack · env vars · scripts · screenshots · contact

bullets: Prompt — 'Generate a README.md for this repository. Sections — title with project tagline, build and test badges, 30-second quickstart (clone → install → env → run), feature list with one-line each, tech stack table, environment variable table with descriptions, npm scripts table, three inline screenshots from /docs/screenshots, contact information.'
Constraints — 'Use GitHub-flavoured Markdown. Restrict emoji usage to headings. Code blocks include language tags. Tables are aligned.'
AI produces — approximately 300 lines of README that reads as senior-engineered. Edit lightly for accuracy; commit; push.
Bonus prompt — 'Add a one-paragraph DESIGN.md explaining the architectural decisions and OGE compliance.' Reviewers respond favourably to this addition.
slides.memory_hook: Eight-section README plus one DESIGN.md = repository presentation reads as senior engineering. Reviewer response is favourable.
slides.closing_thread: Push the repository. Share the URL. Submission is complete.

slides.title: Six-Module Recap — Capabilities Acquired
slides.subtitle: From practitioner to OrchestrAI Lead in approximately six hours
items: Module 1 · The Mindset — orchestration over execution. AI implements; the Lead directs. The conductor analogy.
Module 2 · The Framework — six lifecycle stages: Intent → Orchestrate → Generate → Validate → Evolve → Deploy.
Module 3 · The Bible — OGE (Observability · Guardrails · Evaluation), Approach A versus B, the two master prompts (T1 plus T2).
Module 4 · Foundation Build — six manual installations, eight-component authentication prompt, shell and dashboard with UI Specifications honoured.
Module 5 · Workflow Engine — sixteen-transition matrix, structured workflow prompt, surgical re-prompts, Git discipline.
Module 6 · Going Live — admin surfaces, reports, QA and UAT co-working, README and DESIGN, GitHub submission. (Current position.)
slides.memory_hook: Six modules · approximately six hours · one reusable playbook for every AI-accelerated build.
slides.closing_thread: We address the capability set this certification provides.
